The King rail (Rallus elegans) is a large, secretive marsh bird inhabiting freshwater wetlands across eastern North America. Field studies have documented that eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require approximately 22 days [ab = approximately 22 days] to hatch, a developmental period that aligns closely with the incubation durations reported for other rallid species of comparable body size. Newly hatched chicks, known as nestlings, emerge weighing an average of 14.7 grams [Wwb = 14.7 grams], reflecting the modest energy reserves contained within the relatively small egg. This initial mass is typical for semi-precocial young that rely on rapid parental provisioning to fuel their subsequent growth. The hatchlings are covered in black down and are capable of leaving the nest within hours, though they depend on adults for thermoregulation and feeding during their first days of life. Brood sizes are variable, but females typically produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], with each clutch containing 10 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 10 eggs], a reproductive strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity given the high energetic demands of chick rearing in these complex marsh environments.

Under the warm thermal conditions characteristic of the species' active season, approximately 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], the developmental trajectory of King rail chicks follows a predictable sequence. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at 30 days after hatching [tx = 30 days after hatching], allowing the young to escape aquatic predators and begin exploring their habitat more independently at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. Shortly after this milestone, the initial wet weight of the nestling at emergence from the egg, recorded as 19.5 grams [Ww0 = 19.5 grams], has typically increased many times over through the relentless feeding efforts of both parents. This value represents the mass of the newly hatched chick immediately after drying, a metric sometimes distinguished from the birth weight recorded at first feeding. The rapid mass gain observed during the nestling period is critical for the development of flight muscles and feather tracts required for fledging. Survival to this stage depends on consistent prey availability and the absence of prolonged flooding events. The relatively late fledging age for a bird of its size is thought to be an adaptation to the complex physical demands of foraging within dense stands of cattail and bulrush.

Sexual maturity in the King rail is attained surprisingly quickly for a long-lived marsh bird. Under the same optimal temperature regime of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], which facilitates peak metabolic performance during the breeding season, individuals reach puberty at 90 days after hatching [tp = 90 days after hatching]. This remarkably short interval from hatching to gonadal activation allows young birds born early in the breeding season to potentially contribute to the population before the year ends. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 340 grams [Wwi = approximately 340 grams], a robust mass that supports the bird's sedentary lifestyle and its ability to defend territories through loud, resonant vocalizations. Reaching this adult body size requires a sustained period of high food intake, and the rapid onset of reproductive capability suggests that energetic investment in structural growth does not entirely delay the maturation of the reproductive system. This life-history strategy is unusual among rails, which often show delayed maturity and a longer period of juvenile development before entering the breeding population.

First reproduction in the King rail, the initial successful incubation of a clutch, is deferred to a later age. Tracking studies indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning that most individuals do not breed until the spring following their hatching year, even though they are physiologically capable of breeding earlier. at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]This delay likely reflects the challenges of territory acquisition and pair formation in a species with a complex social structure and strong site fidelity. The daily reproduction rate, which integrates clutch size and annual frequency, is effectively very low; the species produces 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 10 eggs per clutch] in a single annual attempt [F_R_i = single annual attempt]. This conservative reproductive output is typical of a K-selected species adapted to stable, though periodically disturbed, wetland environments. The relatively high investment per egg, signaled by the substantial hatchling mass already described, compensates for the small number of offspring produced per breeding season and enhances the survival prospects of each chick.

Longevity records for the King rail are limited, but comparative data from the closely related American coot (Fulica americana) provide a useful benchmark. Based on this analog, the maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 22.3 years [am = approximately 22.3 years], a substantial duration that underscores the slow pace of life in this species when measured against the background temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This estimated longevity, if confirmed in Rallus elegans, would place it among the longer-lived members of the Rallidae, a family generally characterized by moderate to high adult survival rates. The ultimate wet weight recorded for the largest adults in museum collections reaches 340 grams [Wwi = 340 grams], a value that may be approached only by very old or particularly dominant individuals. This connection between extended lifespan and large body size is consistent with broader life-history theory, which predicts that species with high adult survivorship will invest more heavily in somatic maintenance and less in annual reproductive effort. The conservation of this species depends on preserving the large, contiguous marsh tracts that allow individuals to reach old age and maintain stable population dynamics.
